paper_metadata.title: Altered longitudinal structural connectome in paediatric mild traumatic brain injury: an Advancing Concussion Assessment in Paediatrics study

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study utilizes a large, multi-center prospective cohort (A-CAP) with well-defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and a robust comparison group (orthopaedic injury). The sample size is the largest to date for this type of study, and baseline characteristics are thoroughly described.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Children aged 8–16.99 years were recruited from five paediatric emergency departments within 48 h of sustaining a concussion (n = 360; 56% male) or mild orthopaedic injury (n = 196; 62% male).
items.reasoning: The authors clearly define the age range, recruitment source (EDs), and the nature of the injuries for both the TBI and OI groups.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: The A-CAP study recruited children (8–16.99 years of age) within 48 h post-injury from five children's hospital emergency departments in Canada, all members of the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada network.
items.reasoning: Recruitment was prospective and conducted across multiple specialized pediatric centers, reducing the risk of site-specific bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the protocol is referenced (Yeates et al. 2017), the specific calendar dates for the recruitment period are not explicitly stated in this manuscript.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location) are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: five children's hospital emergency departments in Canada... Calgary, Edmonton, Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver
items.reasoning: The specific cities and clinical settings (EDs) are clearly listed.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Children with TBI sustained a blunt head trauma and met at least one of three criteria per the World Health Organization definition of mild TBI... Delayed neurological deterioration (e.g. Glasgow Coma Scale score <13), neurosurgical intervention, loss of consciousness >30 min or post-traumatic amnesia >24 h were exclusionary criteria
items.reasoning: The study uses standardized WHO criteria and provides specific clinical thresholds for exclusion.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide the total number of eligible patients screened versus those who consented (participation rate), making it difficult to assess potential selection bias at the point of entry.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 2 Sample demographic and injury characteristics... Age, Sex, Parental education, Race, Mechanism of injury, Sport-related injury, Loss of consciousness, Glasgow Coma Scale, Prior concussion history
items.reasoning: Table 2 provides a comprehensive breakdown of demographics and injury-related variables for both groups.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Attrition rates are reported and are relatively low for a longitudinal neuroimaging study. The use of Linear Mixed Effects (LME) models helps mitigate the impact of missing data at specific time points.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: Overall study attrition rates (i.e. 15, 25 and 28% for the post-acute, 3- and 6-month assessments, respectively) are consistent with other studies
items.reasoning: A 72% retention rate at 6 months is considered acceptable for this study design.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not describe specific efforts to re-engage or collect data from dropouts.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: the final data set included 882 scans from 556 children after excluding 241 scans (21%; 170 TBI/71 OI) during initial quality assessment due to unstandardized acquisition parameters... severe motion artefact... incomplete acquisition... scanner artefacts... or gross brain structure abnormalities.
items.reasoning: The authors provide detailed reasons for data exclusion (technical/quality issues), but do not explicitly detail the behavioral or personal reasons for participant dropout.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: There is no comparison provided between the characteristics of those who completed the study and those who were lost to follow-up.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The authors do not explicitly state whether they tested for differences between completers and non-completers.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (mild TBI vs OI) is clearly defined using international standards. The sub-classification of TBI (persistent vs non-persistent symptoms) uses a statistically rigorous Reliable Change Index (RCI) based on validated symptom scales.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Children with TBI sustained a blunt head trauma and met at least one of three criteria per the World Health Organization definition of mild TBI.
items.reasoning: The primary prognostic factor (injury group) is well-defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: The Health and Behaviour Inventory, a core measure in the Common Data Elements for paediatric TBI, was used to assess cognitive and somatic symptoms... Premorbid and 1-month post-injury scores were compared to calculate a reliable change index (z-score) score.
items.reasoning: The use of CDE-recommended scales and RCI methodology ensures a reliable classification of the 'persistent symptoms' prognostic factor.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: We then used the reliable change score results to classify children with mild TBI into two groups... (i) TBI with persistent symptoms... and (ii) TBI without persistent symptoms
items.reasoning: The cut-points for symptom persistence are based on a standardized statistical method (RCI) rather than arbitrary data-driven thresholds.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: All participants in the study completed 3 T MRI at the postacute follow-up and were randomly assigned to complete a second MRI scan at the 3 or 6 months (chronic) follow-up.
items.reasoning: The protocol was standardized across all sites and participants.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: the final data set included 882 scans from 556 children
items.reasoning: The majority of the recruited sample provided usable data for the primary analysis.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models were computed... controlling for the random effect of participant.
items.reasoning: LME models are the standard approach for handling missing data in longitudinal studies as they use all available data points without requiring simple imputation.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcomes (graph theory metrics) are derived from advanced neuroimaging using a standardized pipeline. The use of ComBAT for multi-site harmonization is a significant strength that reduces measurement bias across different scanners.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: Global and local (nodal) level metrics included degree, clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, smallworldness, betweenness and degree centrality, and efficiency (for definitions and descriptions, see Table 1)
items.reasoning: The outcomes are mathematically defined and categorized according to graph theory principles.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: network metrics were harmonized for site (scanner) differences using neuroComBAT... This approach can preserve the variability attributable to biological effects of interest... while removing variability due to the use of different scanners.
items.reasoning: The use of deterministic tractography and ComBAT harmonization ensures high reliability of the imaging outcomes across the multi-site design.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Whole-brain diffusion-weighted images were acquired using 30 different gradient directions at b = 900 s/ mm2 and 5 at b = 0 s/mm2 , with 2.2 mm isotropic resolution.
items.reasoning: The acquisition parameters were standardized across sites, and remaining variance was statistically harmonized.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study rigorously accounts for major confounders (age, sex, site) in both the harmonization process and the final statistical models. The inclusion of an orthopaedic injury group specifically controls for the general effects of trauma and ED visit.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: Group, days (time) post-injury, age at injury and sex were included in the covariate matrix during harmonization.
items.reasoning: Key demographic and temporal variables are accounted for.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: Age [Mean (SD) years]... Sex [n (%) male]... Mechanism of injury
items.reasoning: Confounders are clearly defined and reported in Table 2.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Details about children's acute clinical presentation were recorded in the emergency department. Mechanism of injury and a demographic questionnaire were collected at the post-acute follow-up.
items.reasoning: Confounders were measured using clinical records and standardized questionnaires.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: The A-CAP study recruited children... from five children's hospital emergency departments... Mechanism of injury and a demographic questionnaire were collected at the post-acute follow-up.
items.reasoning: The data collection protocol was uniform across the study.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models were computed
items.reasoning: LME models handle missingness in covariates effectively within the longitudinal framework.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: This study compared the structural connectome of children with concussion to those with mild orthopaedic injury
items.reasoning: The use of an OI group is a design-level control for the confounding effects of general injury and medical stress.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: The final model is given by the following formulas... Group x (Time + Time2) x (Age + Sex) + Hemisphere + (1|Participant)
items.reasoning: The statistical models explicitly adjust for age, sex, time, and site (via harmonization).

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach is sophisticated and appropriate for longitudinal imaging data. The authors use FDR correction to manage the high volume of comparisons and report effect sizes (Cohen's d) with confidence intervals, which aids in interpreting clinical significance.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models were computed in RStudio using the lmerTest package... The final model is given by the following formulas
items.reasoning: The authors provide the exact mathematical formulas and software packages used.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: The strategy for model building... is based on a conceptual framework or model... Group, days (time) post-injury, age at injury and sex were included
items.reasoning: The model includes biologically relevant interactions (e.g., age and sex) known to influence brain development and injury recovery.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: Multiple linear mixed effects models were computed... to investigate the relations of group... controlling for the random effect of participant.
items.reasoning: LME is the gold standard for longitudinal data with varying time points and missing observations.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: Correction for multiple comparisons was conducted using the false discovery rate (FDR) at corrected P < 0.05... Only effects with a 95% confidence interval range for d that excluded 0 were considered to be robust
items.reasoning: The authors report both significant and non-significant findings (e.g., global metrics) and use stringent correction methods to prevent false positives.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
